limelight. A goodly number of
sizeable fish have been taken since
last Saturday when Capt. Rodie
Langley and his party consisting
of DR.. and Mrs. Dave Sherry. their
son Mark, and Mr.. and Mrs.
Walter Herman landed Is nice
ones.


Although a few scattered hard
heads have been caught, this
species, which last season was
scarce in bay waters, has yet to
show signs of a comeback. Con-
sidering the prolonged cool
weather this spring, it is still a
little early. Until the last two
years, hardheads had given the
most sport to the most anglers
here for several decades. Those
seeking them this year are taking
a few white perch which have
finished their spawning runs and
returned to salt water, but toad
fish and eels have been their main
catch.


Channel bass anglers who have
journeyed to Oregon Inlet and
vicinity this season have run into
much windy weather and few fish.
Last week end was no exception,
dry northeaster churning the
waters. A few blues were caught
off the piers at Nags Head over
the week end in spite of windy
weather and also a few rockfish
were taken trolling in the sound.


Heavy waters following the ex-
tensive rainfall of a fortnight ago
have run their course and most
mountain trout streams in both
Maryland and Virginia have re-
turned to normal. There are
plenty of good fish to be caught
in both States and barring heavy
rainfall on headwaters, this week
end should prove a bonanza to
those who like to cast a fly or
float an angleworm.

The case of Inspector Albert I. Bullock poses
a difficult problem for Major Murray, the newly
installed Superintendent Of Police.


Inspector Bullock was indicted in the Nelson
gambling conspiracy case and acquitted by
directed verdict. The statute of limitations was
the controlling consideration in that verdict,
but it might not be a controlling factor in trial
board action by the Superintendent of Police
and the Commissioners. The question of what
action Of this Sort If any, might be taken against
INSPECTOR Bullock is now under investigation by
competent and respected committee Of the
District Bar Association.


Meanwhile, the inspector has dragged his
feet in replying to QUESTIONABLE sent him by
the Senate District Crime Committee. Possibly
there might be basis in this for disciplinary
action, but surely it is of small Importance when
compared to the action which may be taken
after the report of the bar associations COM
mittee has been made.


Major Murray evidently wants to await that
report before deciding on his next move, and
it seems to The Star that this is the right
attitude. He inherited this situation in the
Police Department. and there is no known
reason to believe that he will not deal with it
firmly and in fairness to all concerned. If he
wants to work the problem out in his own way,
he should have an opportunity to do it. The
thing by which his performance should be judged
is the end result-not by the test of whether
he acts hastily and, perhaps, rashly.
